description: Down in the basement the practical bench is lined with first-years' boilers, each waiting for a qualified hand to test it before it is lit. The first-years are still testing. It is gone nine, and nobody has eaten since a bun at noon. A spirit stove sits at the end of the bench beside a dented pot, and a row of hollow-eyed faces turns toward you as the only person present who has been seen to cook.

options.label: Make supper from whatever is in the cupboard, and hope the pot forgives you.

success.text: It is brown, thick and shapeless, and it is gone in four minutes. Someone scrapes the pot with a spanner. Two portions are wrapped in the Gazette and pressed into your hands for the road, with the solemnity usually reserved for pensions.

failure.text: The pot catches, and so does your sleeve. The smell is brought up in a lecture the following week as an example of incomplete combustion. The first-years eat bread and look at you kindly, which is worse.

options.label: Stir two measures of your barley meal into a proper porridge for the bench.

success.text: The porridge is plain and hot and exactly enough. The bench eats in a silence broken only by spoons and, once, a boiler ticking as it cools. Somebody writes your name in the margin of a pressure table, for reasons of gratitude.

options.label: Fry two cuts of your salt pork, and take a ration from the bench's thanks.

success.text: The pork spits across the stove, and the basement smells for an hour of better days. The first-years eat standing, still holding their gauges. One leaves a Rustmoor ration on the pot lid, wrapped in a lab sheet, without a word.
